Tried one search and found it impressive. The user has been using elicit.com, which they feel takes a less AI-heavy approach, and plans to give Undermind a shot for a few months.

Mixed result on a very niche query: the first search missed what they wanted, and a refined second search returned nearly the same results. It seemed to over-rely on citation count, still surfacing papers the user said they weren't interested in. Few dissertations or theses appeared, though some relevant ones exist. It did surface some interesting tangential papers.
Found it more effective than crawling with Google Scholar.
An independent researcher without an academic email address couldn't sign up.

Meta-analysis author: after good follow-up questions, top results included studies in their dataset plus one new study they'd missed. It missed a sample-size exclusion, didn't link a protocol to its study, and missed much gray literature. Their lab could pay for it, but not as the only search method.

A CS academic found two items in the top 10 results that they should have found themselves, from their own community. There were some irrelevant results and many already-known ones, but overall they were very impressed and will use it again.
Pretty good: it found some useful references the user had missed in Google Scholar and arXiv.

Compared with Claude 3.5 Sonnet: Claude is reluctant to give references unless coaxed, while Undermind solves this. It helped refine a question on longitudinal brain volume studies and returned 100 ranked, lightly annotated citations with topic-match scores.
A marketer (CRM) found it useful for finding research applicable to their field, though nothing particularly new was surfaced.
Queries take an excruciatingly long time to return results.
A very happy subscriber who searches a lot. Since their usage will drop, they won't keep paying $20/month, and they'd like a pay-per-query option at $1-3 per extended query.
Been using Undermind for several months; it's been a lifesaver for getting a comprehensive understanding of a research topic.
Complaint: the requirement to use a valid institutional or company email address is an obnoxious, unnecessary roadblock.
Skeptical of the approach (GPT-4 as a cross-encoder seems wasteful). Called 3-6 minute searches brutal, since low latency matters for letting users reformulate queries.
'Try it now' leads to a sign-up with no social sign-in. Branding and design feel less trustworthy than Elicit's, and the name evokes 'undermine'.

Searched protein inhibitors for cancer treatment and found at least 4 new informative papers after 3 months of searching ScienceDirect and PubMed. In under six minutes it gave more relevant results than about a week of ScienceDirect searching. Liked the clean results page; the home page is lacking.

The best results the user has gotten from an AI research assistant. They don't mind the long latency, seeing it as better than Bing/Perplexity-style RAG with uneven results, and like that longer prompts beat keyword fiddling. The 'Discovery Progress and Exhaustiveness' section (e.g., 23.6% of relevant papers found) was confusing.
